summary: This standards-track document defines SLURM, a way for local network operators to adjust the RPKI data they use for BGP route validation. The RPKI lets resource holders make verifiable statements about Internet number resources. SLURM lets an operator add or filter such information locally.

eli5.summary: You have a shared list of rules, but you can add a few notes of your own in the margin. SLURM is the notes.

questions: how to locally override rpki data
subtitle: A small JSON file that lets a network operator filter and add to the RPKI data its own routers see.

tldr.problem: The global RPKI cannot verify private address space or private AS numbers, and an operator may also want to override RPKI data it believes was changed by an adverse action. Operators needed a standard way to make local exceptions.
tldr.mechanism: SLURM is a JSON file with two parts: Validation Output Filters that remove matching data from what the Relying Party sends to routers, and Locally Added Assertions that add ROA prefix and BGPsec data. The effect is applied atomically.
tldr.outcome: The exceptions apply only locally and do not change how other operators read the RPKI. The RFC warns that an error in a SLURM file can undermine the security the RPKI offers that operator.

today: RFC 8416 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Local Overrides Are Needed
sections.content:
The Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) lets the holder of Internet number resources make verifiable statements about them. For example, the holder of a block of addresses can issue a Route Origin Authorization (ROA) that authorizes an Autonomous System to originate routes for that block. Internet Service Providers can then use the RPKI to validate BGP routes, both the origin of a route (RFC 6811) and its path (RFC 8205).

A Relying Party (RP) may still want to override what the repositories say. RFC 6491 recommends ROAs that invalidate public routes for reserved and unallocated space, yet some ISPs want to use BGP and the RPKI with private address space or private AS numbers. That use is legitimate but cannot be verified by the global RPKI. An operator might also want to protect routes from adverse actions (RFC 8211) until the results are addressed.

The mechanisms are called SLURM. They work on two kinds of assertion. For origin validation, an assertion is a tuple of IP prefix, prefix length, maximum length and ASN. For BGPsec, it is a tuple of ASN, subject key identifier and router public key. The RFC calls these ROA Prefix Assertions and BGPsec Assertions.
sections.eli5: The big public rule book cannot know about your private clubhouse. SLURM lets you write your own small notes so your own computers know about it.

sections.title: Where SLURM Sits in the Relying Party
sections.content:
An RP with SLURM filters out, meaning removes from consideration for routing decisions, any assertions in the RPKI that are overridden by local ROA Prefix Assertions and BGPsec Assertions.

The main output of an RP is the data it sends to routers over the RPKI-Router protocol (RFC 8210). Routers can ask for everything (a Reset Query) or only for changes (a Serial Query). SLURM is applied to the result set of a Reset Query, and to both the old and new sets that are compared for a Serial Query. Other forms of RP output may be modified in comparable ways, but that is outside the scope of the document.

In the RFC's Figure 1, data flows from the repositories to a local cache of RPKI objects, then to validation, then through the SLURM filters, then the SLURM assertions, then the RPKI-Router protocol and finally to BGP speakers.
sections.eli5: Think of an assembly line. The public list comes down the belt, SLURM crosses out a few items and writes in a few more, and only then does the list go to the routers.

sections.title: The SLURM File
sections.content:
SLURM filters and assertions are written in JSON (RFC 8259). JSON members not defined in the RFC MUST NOT be used, and an RP MUST treat any deviation as an error. Future additions MUST use an incremented value for the slurmVersion member.

A SLURM file is a single JSON object with these members:

  • slurmVersion, which MUST be the number 1.
  • validationOutputFilters, an object that MUST contain exactly two members, prefixFilters and bgpsecFilters.
  • locallyAddedAssertions, an object that MUST contain exactly two members, prefixAssertions and bgpsecAssertions.

In the typical case an RP uses both parts. The result MUST be the same as if output filtering were performed before locally adding assertions, so Locally Added Assertions MUST NOT be removed by output filtering.
sections.eli5: A SLURM file is a form with four boxes: two for things to cross out and two for things to add. Any box can be left empty.

sections.title: Validation Output Filters
sections.content:
Filters remove data. A Prefix Filter holds an IPv4 or IPv6 prefix, an ASN, or both. Any Validated ROA Payload (VRP) that matches a configured Prefix Filter MUST be removed from the RP's output. A VRP matches if:

  • the filter has only a prefix and the VRP prefix is equal to or covered by it;
  • the filter has only an ASN and the VRP ASN matches it; or
  • the filter has both, and both conditions hold.

A BGPsec Filter works the same way using an ASN, a Router Subject Key Identifier (SKI), or both. The SKI is the Base64 encoding, without trailing =, of the certificate's Subject Key Identifier. Any BGPsec Assertion that matches a configured BGPsec Filter MUST be removed.

Each filter MAY carry one optional comment string, and including a comment is RECOMMENDED so that it can be shown to users of the RP software.
sections.eli5: A filter is a list of things to cross out: this street, this person, or this person on this street. Anything that matches gets crossed out.

sections.title: Locally Added Assertions
sections.content:
Assertions add data. A ROA Prefix Assertion MUST contain an IPv4 or IPv6 prefix and an ASN. It MAY include a maxPrefixLength number and a comment. The combination of prefix, ASN and optional maximum length describes a VRP, and the RP MUST add all such assertions to the VRPs found through RPKI validation. It must then send the complete set of PDUs over the RPKI-Router protocol, excluding duplicates.

A BGPsec Assertion MUST contain an asn, an SKI and a routerPublicKey. The public key is the Base64 encoding, without trailing =, of the full ASN.1 DER encoding of the subjectPublicKeyInfo. This matches the syntax of the Router Key PDU in RFC 8210, and RPs MUST add these to the set of Router Key PDUs, excluding duplicates.

Because filtering is conceptually done first, an assertion you add is never removed by one of your own filters.
sections.eli5: Assertions are the things you write into the margin: here is a route I know is real, even though the big list does not mention it.

sections.title: Atomicity and Multiple Files
sections.content:
The effect of SLURM MUST be atomic. The RP output either MUST be the same as if no SLURM file were used or MUST reflect the entire configuration. The RFC gives an example: two local routes for the same prefix with different origin ASNs, both configured with Locally Added Assertions. If neither addition occurs, both routes could be NotFound. If both occur, both are Valid. If only one occurs, one could be Invalid while the other is Valid.

An implementation MAY support several SLURM files at once. The inputs to the filters and assertions are then the unions of those from each file. This is meant for files with distinct scopes, for example operators of two networks who share one RP system.

Before using files from different sources, the RP MUST make sure there is no internal conflict among them. If it finds overlaps, in prefix assertions and filters that cover the same IP address, or in BGPsec assertions and filters that use the same ASN, the whole set MUST be rejected, and the RP SHOULD issue a warning as an error report.
sections.eli5: Either all of your notes count, or none of them do. Half your notes would make the map confusing, so the helper never does half.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
SLURM gives an operator more control over RPKI data while preserving autonomy over address space and ASN management. It is applied only locally and does not influence how other operators interpret RPKI data. Even so, care is needed: SLURM can also be used to locally change assertions about non-private resources, such as globally routed space, for example to override data the operator believes was corrupted by an adverse action. The RFC says operators who do this should use extreme caution.

An RP using a SLURM file is trusting what is in it. Errors can undermine the security the RPKI offers that RP, since a file could declare ROAs invalid that would otherwise be valid, and vice versa. The RP MUST carefully consider the security implications, especially if a third party provides the file.

Each RP MUST also ensure the authenticity and integrity of any SLURM file it uses, including updates received over the network. The mechanism for that is out of scope. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Your own notes are powerful, so a wrong note can fool your own computers. Make sure nobody sneaks a fake note into your list.
